Citizen Kane. Orson Welles' landmark film that chronicles the rise and fall of Charles Foster Kane, a newspaper magnate and media tycoon, through multiple perspectives and flashbacks.

Charles Foster Kane grows from a poor boy into a newspaper publisher and media mogul who shapes American public opinion through propaganda. The film opens with Kane's death and the mystery of his final word: Rosebud. Reporters attempt to decode this cryptic utterance, convinced it holds the key to understanding who Kane really was.

Through interviews and flashbacks, Kane's life unfolds. His marriages and infidelities. His political campaigns and affairs. The accumulation of wealth and art. Kane is portrayed as increasingly isolated, manipulative, and consumed by his own power, despite moments of apparent vulnerability. His trajectory is one of ambition and corruption, a man who seemingly has everything but loses himself in pursuit of control.

The final scene delivers the twist. Rosebud is not a woman, a political rival, or a hidden treasure. It is Kane's childhood sled. The symbol of lost innocence before his ambition and power consumed him. This simple wooden sled represents the last memory of happiness, before he was sent away to pursue wealth and reinvent himself as a titan of industry.

The sled is then burned at the end of the film, destroyed without anyone knowing its significance. The revelation suggests that Kane's essential humanity was irretrievable. The mystery that everyone sought to solve is revealed only in its final moments, and then it is destroyed, just as Kane destroyed himself in pursuit of power.

Released in nineteen forty-one, the film is considered one of cinema's greatest achievements. It pioneered multiple-narrator structure and non-linear editing in mainstream cinema. The twist recontextualizes Kane's entire trajectory as the tragedy of a man who lost his humanity, asking whether some truths about a life are ultimately unknowable.
